pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Blueberry Anthracnose is caused by the fungus Colletotrichum acutatum.

type_of_disease.quote: Anthracnose fruit rot is a common fungal disease of blueberries in all growing regions of the U.S.

value: Fruit
Foliar
Stem
Seed
affected_parts.quote: Blueberry Anthracnose (aka â€˜ripe rotâ€™), primarily damages fruit but may also infect twigs and spurs.

summary.value: The first symptoms are fruit softening and shriveled areas near the calyx (blossom) end, followed by small sticky orange/salmon spore masses (conidia) that grow and can envelop the whole fruit.
summary.quote: The first visible symptoms are fruit softening and the development of shriveled areas near the calyx (blossom) end of the fruit. Small orange spots begin to appear in these shriveled areas shortly after initial symptom development and continue to grow in size and number.

diagnostic_features.value: Infected fruit shows bright pink to salmon/orange spore masses (conidia) produced from acervuli that break through the fruit's skin at the blossom end, typically appearing on mature fruit after ripening ("ripe rot"); sunken lesions develop and neighboring berries may be infected yet remain asymptomatic.
diagnostic_features.quote: Infected fruit shows bright pink spore masses at the blossom end. Stem cankers with raised purple margins can occur but are rare.

value: Phomopsis canker and twig blight
Botrytis blossom blight
look_alikes.quote: These symptoms can often be confused with other fungal diseases of highbush blueberry, including Phomopsis canker and twig blight and Botrytis blossom blight.

value: Select less susceptible / resistant cultivars before planting (e.g. 'Elliott', 'Legacy', 'Reveille'; moderately resistant 'Draper'/'Elliott'); emphasize cultivars with dry stem scars and those that drop bud scales earlier in spring

Prune bushes and use wide plant spacing to open the canopy and improve airflow, reducing moisture duration and humidity; selectively prune off dead buds, pedicels, twigs, trusses, and canes (in fall/winter) and remove/destroy prunings
Use drip irrigation to avoid wetting aerial plant parts; if using overhead irrigation, water early in the day so plants dry before nightfall
Harvest frequently (at least every 7 days) to limit overripe fruit; do not harvest or handle fruit when wet
Refrigerate/cool harvested fruit promptly (around 35Â°F / 2Â°C within two hours of harvest; forced-air cooling for palletized fruit) to reduce postharvest fruit rots
Keep equipment and containers clean and dry before contact with berries
Apply preventative fungicides when scouting and weather indicate risk; sprays beginning at full bloom and repeating every 7-14 days through harvest are most effective
Rotate fungicide active ingredients from different FRAC groups to avoid resistance development
Scout fields beginning at bloom and consult prior-year scouting records; monitor weather to identify likely infection periods
treatments.quote: Preventative fungicides can be used to minimize the sources of infection in the field. Sprays beginning at full bloom and repeating every 7-14 days through harvest are most effective

conflicts.note: NC State attributes the disease to two species complexes, C. acutatum and C. gloeosporioides, rather than C. acutatum alone.

Rutgers identifies C. fioriniae (a member of the C. acutatum species complex) as the primary causal organism in New Jersey, with other species from the C. gloeosporioides complex also able to infect. No NCBI/MycoBank validation was supplied to resolve the canonical name.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: In Florida, the fungus Thekopsora minima causes leaf rust on SHB.

type_of_disease.quote: information for Florida blueberry growers on the disease cycle, symptoms, and integrated management of this fungal leaf disease

value: Foliar
affected_parts.quote: Leaf rust symptoms are initially observed as small, somewhat angular yellow spots, turning red to black on the upper surfaces of leaves.

summary.value: First symptoms are small, chlorotic to yellow spots; spots on the upper leaf surface turn reddish-brown and leaves may die if spots coalesce and become necrotic. On the leaf underside, yellowish-orange pustules (uredinia) develop that turn rusty-red with age, and infected leaves usually drop prematurely.
summary.quote: The first symptoms observe include small, chlorotic to yellow spots. Spots on the upper surface of the leaf turn reddish-brown. The entire leaf may die if numerous spots coalesce and become necrotic. On the underside of the leaf, opposite upper leaf symptoms, yellowish-orange pustules (uredinia) develop that turn rusty-red with age. Infected leaves usually drop prematurely.

diagnostic_features.value: Dusty clumps of yellow-, orange-, or rust-colored spores (urediniospores) on the underside of the leaf, opposite the upper leaf lesions; when present these spores distinguish leaf rust from all other leaf spot diseases. Lesions can be limited by larger leaf veins, resulting in lesions with parallel straight or angular sides.
diagnostic_features.quote: When present, these spores are a key feature distinguishing leaf rust from all other leaf spot diseases (Figure 2).

value: Other leaf spot diseases
look_alikes.quote: these spores are a key feature distinguishing leaf rust from all other leaf spot diseases

value: Integrate horticultural and chemical methods to reduce the impact of the disease.
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead irrigation where and whenever possible.
When overhead irrigation is necessary, time the application to avoid extended periods of leaf wetness and to occur after dew formation in early morning hours.
Plant spacing, maintenance pruning to increase airflow in the canopy, and controlling weeds in row middles.
Remove hemlocks upwind from where blueberry is grown.
Grow less susceptible cultivars.
Prompt removal and disposal of fallen leaves may be helpful.
Make repeated fungicide applications to maintain a protective residue on the leaves; scout during post-bloom and early fall periods.
Chemical control: start when leaves first begin to break bud and unfold; continue at regular intervals during wet weather.
chlorothalonil (e.g., Bravo TM / Bravo Weather Stik, Group M5; after harvest only) applications for rust management can begin late fall, before bloom.
Proline TM / Proline 480 SC (prothioconazole), an excellent DMI choice for rust (seven-day PHI).
Quilt Xcel TM / QuiltXcel (azoxystrobin and propiconazole, Group 3 + 11).
Propulse TM (fluopyram and prothioconazole, Group 3 + 7).
Other DMIs with longer preharvest intervals if rust increases before bloom (e.g., Indar TM, Tilt TM).
Quash TM for flare-ups closer to harvest.
Quadris Flowable / Quadris Top and Pristine TM have rust efficacy and make good rotation partners with a DMI product.
Consider tank mixing a captan product with Quadris Flowable or Pristine TM.
Bordeaux 8-8-100 plus spreader-sticker; copper products (e.g., Kocide 50 DF, Nu-Cop 50 DF) â€” not for use in the spring.
Inspire Super (Group 3 + 9).
Regalia (Group P5) â€” may be used day of harvest.
Organic management options include copper products and plant-based horticultural oils.
Biological control: Sonata (Bacillus pumilis strain QST 2808) plus a spreader-sticker; may be applied up to and including the day of harvest.
Fungicides with different modes of action should be used in rotation or in a tank mix as part of an integrated postharvest foliage management strategy.
treatments.quote: The best strategies to efficiently manage rust integrate horticultural and chemical methods to reduce the impact of the disease

conflicts.alternative_value: Thekopsora minima and Naohidemyces vaccinii (both formerly Pucciniastrum vaccinii)
conflicts.note: The UF/IFAS source attributes Florida SHB leaf rust to Thekopsora minima alone; the PNW handbook lists two causal fungi (Thekopsora minima and Naohidemyces vaccinii), both formerly classified as Pucciniastrum vaccinii. No taxonomy validation was supplied to adjudicate.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Mummy berry is caused by the fungus Monilinia vaccinii-corymbosi.

type_of_disease.quote: Mummy berry is a fungal disease common among blueberry species in North America.

value: Foliar
Stem
affected_parts.quote: Mummy berry is a disease of blueberry that affects both leaf shoots and berries.

summary.value: Infected shoots wilt with browning of the midrib and veins, and a mass of ash-gray conidia forms along the leaf midrib; infected berries turn salmon-pink (or pink/cream) with soft deteriorating skin and a hard fungal structure inside, eventually drying to whitish-gray hard mummies that fall to the ground.
summary.quote: The next visible symptom occurs at harvest, when infected berries (mummies) turn a salmon-pink color, with soft deteriorating skin and a hard fungal structure (pseudosclerotium) inside.

diagnostic_features.value: Berries do not turn blue but instead turn pink or salmon-colored, with soft deteriorating skin and a hard fungal structure (pseudosclerotium) inside; blighted leaf shoots produce a mass of ash-gray conidia along the leaf midrib; cup-shaped apothecia ("mummy cups") emerge from old infected berries on the ground in spring.
diagnostic_features.quote: A further diagnostic sign of the pathogen is the production of a mass of ash-gray conidia (spores) along the midrib of the leaves on blighted leaf shoots.

value: Raking, cultivating, and/or mulching underneath blueberry bushes can bury mummies and reduce further spread
Rotating between different active ingredients prevents the evolution of fungicide resistance
Planting only disease-free, dormant plants
Sanitation can be used to reduce the incidence and severity of disease by removing or burying the overwintering mummies
Hand raking or the use of a leaf blower around bushes can be used to move mummies to the aisles between rows where they can be disked under or collected with a bagging mower
Mulch applied 3-4 inches deep underneath bushes will prevent mummies from emerging in Spring
Fungicides are used at leaf emergence to prevent primary (leaf shoot) infection, and again during bloom to prevent secondary (flower) infection
Plant resistant cultivars (rabbiteye: Premier, Columbus, Powderblue; southern highbush: Legacy, O'Neal, Star; northern highbush: Duke, Elliot)
treatments.quote: Fungicides are used at leaf emergence to prevent primary (leaf shoot) infection, and again during bloom to prevent secondary (flower) infection.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Dieback symptoms of twig blight of blueberry, caused by the fungus Phomopsis vaccinii.

type_of_disease.quote: Twig blight is a fungal disease

value: Stem
Vascular
affected_parts.quote: conidia become trapped in opening buds, germinate, and infect the vascular system

summary.value: Individual buds turn brown and die, followed by browning and necrosis of bark around the bud as the fungus spreads into the twig, causing dieback of fruit-bearing twigs.
summary.quote: Individual buds turn brown and die, followed by browning and necrosis of bark around the bud as the fungus spreads from the blighted bud into the twig.

diagnostic_features.value: The disease stops progressing after killing the twig (6-10 inches) and does not progress further down the stem to infect older wood; pycnidia are evident in diseased tissues.
diagnostic_features.quote: The disease stops progressing after killing the twig (6-10 inches), and does not progress further down the stem to infect older wood.

value: Pruning can be performed to remove infected twigs prior to spore release in the spring
Commercial growers who mow bushes in June and July after harvest (topping) will also benefit from the removal of blighted twigs
Careful cultivar selection can greatly reduce the amount of twig blight experienced; newer cultivars (Legacy, New Hanover, O'Neal, Star, Farthing) are generally resistant to twig blight
Chemical control can be achieved by spraying labeled fungicides from budbreak through bloom on a 7-14 day interval
treatments.quote: 1. Pruning can be performed to remove infected twigs prior to spore release in the spring. This will decrease the amount of disease inoculum present at budbreak.

conflicts.note: University of Maine titles this disease 'Phomopsis Canker and Twig Blight' (combining the twig blight and cane canker stages of Phomopsis vaccinii); NCSU names the twig blight stage 'Twig Blight of Blueberry'. Merged as the same Phomopsis disease.

conflicts.canonical_value: The disease stops progressing after killing the twig (6-10 inches) and does not progress further down the stem to infect older wood; pycnidia are evident in diseased tissues.
conflicts.note: UMaine contributes the diagnostic sign of pycnidia in diseased tissues; NCSU contributes the twig-killing/dieback diagnostic. Both incorporated into the canonical value.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Phomopsis vaccinii also causes a fruit rot on blueberry at harvest in North Carolina.

type_of_disease.quote: Fruit rot caused by Phomopsis vaccinii, the same fungus that causes twig blight of blueberry.

value: Fruit
affected_parts.quote: Phomopsis vaccinii also causes a fruit rot on blueberry at harvest in North Carolina.

summary.value: Infected berries become very soft and may split, resulting in leakage of juice.
summary.quote: Infected berries become very soft and may split resulting in leakage of juice.

value: Most other varieties can be grown with minimal loss due to the fruit rot stage if fruit is harvested in a timely fashion to avoid overripe fruit on the bush
In North Carolina, fruiting bushes should be harvested every 7 days or less
treatments.quote: Most other varieties can be grown with minimal loss due to the fruit rot stage if fruit is harvested in a timely fashion to avoid overripe fruit on the bush. In North Carolina, fruiting bushes should be harvested every 7 days or less.
